Which numbers can you cite?

Each fact is a short statement quoted verbatim from a source in the research database, rated on two independent scales: how politically noteworthy it is for progressive advocacy, and how truthful its evidence is.

Welcome to our AI dashboard.

The AI transition is one of the most challenging transformations of our times. We don’t know what this technology will become, or what policy should do in response.

Each question calls for a different kind of answer, which is how this dashboard is organized. We’re learning here alongside everyone else, but we think what we’ve built can contribute to a better AI transition.

Research

It’s unclear how the technology itself will take shape. Will it be a normal technology, as Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue, or is it more like electricity, where the whole economy eventually reorganizes around it?

Our research tracker is a searchable, tagged list of work on AI and its impact, broadly defined. Alongside it is our fact bank, meant as a resource for the community as a whole: specific sentences you can consider using, each with a caveat section laying out what the finding actually supports and where it has been stretched.

How this section is built. Our team selects priority research and aims to add to it every month. To cover this much ground, Claude pulls the facts and drafts the summaries, and a person reviews them: each fact says which model extracted it, and each summary says whether it has been reviewed yet. We’ve built skills to check the output for accuracy, but as with any secondhand source, verify anything you plan to cite or build on. Terminal-based AI tools are becoming more important for ideas-based work, and we’d rather experiment with putting them into our own workflow than only write about them.

Policy

And even then, it’s hard to know how to react. What policies safeguard against the downsides, amplify what’s good, and make sure this broadly helps people? Should we work through the policies we already have, or does a genuinely new era demand bigger and different ideas? How much can we steer the technology, and how much should we just plan on absorbing its effects?

Our policy map includes nearly every idea people have raised for making AI safe and broadly beneficial. Click through any of them and you’ll find the major bills and initiatives from that policy’s advocates.

This is also where we build on our theory of provoking and legitimizing policy solutions. In a world where AI is fundamentally disruptive, the work is provocation: ideas that go well beyond shoring up what we already have. In a world where AI mostly accelerates the prosperity and the inequality of the last several decades, the work is legitimation, and that’s the harder job. We already know what those solutions look like. They have been contested for thirty years.

How this section is built. Every policy card is written by someone from our team, and we aim to review the policies every quarter.

Government action

Meanwhile, governments are already acting. What are Congress and the states actually putting on the table, and where does each bill stand? What has been enforced under the laws we already have, and what have the courts said?

On the map, point at a state to see what is happening there, from where its bills stand, introduced to enacted, to the cases and enforcement actions listed for it, then follow the links in its card to the full lists, which you can search by view (legislation, enforcement and cases) and filter by topic (and, for bills, by status).

How this section is built. Federal bills, listed when its title names AI or is a close relative of it, come from GovInfo’s bill-status data. Congressional Research Service provides summaries for federal bills where it has written one. State bills and their summaries come from Open States, which follows each legislature’s record. Enforcement and case entries are chosen by the team and brief descriptions are pulled from the agency’s or court’s page. We aim to refresh the bills every week and to update the enforcement actions and cases every month. Topics are our reading of each bill’s title and summary, so check a bill’s official record before you cite it.
